question: (a) Define the term 'Society'. (b) “Human beings cannot live in isolation, but in a society”. Assign four reasons to support this statement.
idealAnswer: A Society is a group of people who conceive of themselves as distinct from other groups and who are connected together through communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics; what makes human societies different from groups of other social animals is that their members share a sense of common identity growing out of a shared culture. More fully, Society may be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good. Society is not a physical thing; the only thing physical about it is the members and their action. Four reasons may be given why human beings live in societies rather than in isolation. First, people abhor solitude and crave companionship: we spontaneously seek others and enjoy their company, whereas loneliness sets up a veritable hunger in the soul. Secondly, we cannot take care of ourselves alone; the child must be reared by the parents for many years, and living in the family implies cooperation right from the beginning of each one's life. Thirdly, the gift of language fits us to communicate with one another, to discuss projects of common interest and to agree on means and ends for cooperative effort, so that the ability of speech itself indicates that we are meant to live a social life. Fourthly, intellectual and moral development requires the constant communication of ideas and values among people, an exchange possible only in a Society. Society is therefore essential to humans, and Aristotle is right in saying that “the life of solitude is fit only for a beast or a god”.

Connected by communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics

People abhor solitude and crave companionship

The gift of language fits us to communicate and cooperate
Intellectual and moral development requires exchange of ideas and values, possible only in a Society

question: (a) Explain the term conflict and give an example. (b) Outline five principles of conflict resolution according to Tokunboh Adeyemo.
idealAnswer: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship, whether at home, at work, in the church or in the nation. When people come together regularly, especially where issues of personal significance are involved, differences emerge; and when conflict occurs between people, individually or in groups, they often become angry, hurt, bitter or defensive, so that the conflict may end a relationship or seriously damage it. Conflict is not always destructive: it can have either constructive or destructive results, it spotlights problems that require attention, and it may force clarification of issues and challenge leaders to question the status quo and search for better solutions. Conflicts are also experienced within ourselves, as an inward personal struggle or restlessness of the soul. A Biblical example is the conflict between the Greeks and the Jews in the Early Church in Jerusalem, whose good handling resulted in the rapid growth of the Church (Acts 6:1-7). In his article in the Africa Bible Commentary, Tokunboh Adeyemo explains that to manage a conflict is simply to organize, regulate and take charge of it in order to make it serve a good cause, and he proposes five guiding principles. The first is honest communication, since silence and isolation deepen misunderstanding: Abraham did not gloss over the potential for quarrels between his herdsmen and Lot's but discussed it openly (Gen. 13:1-18). The second is getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives, because the apparent cause of a conflict is often not the real issue, as with Isaac and the people of Gerar, whose real problem went beyond water (Gen. 26:19-31). The third is negotiation, a process of give and take in which neither party insists on being the winner; Rehoboam's unwillingness to negotiate had disastrous consequences (1 Kings 12). The fourth is external intervention, seeking the assistance of a neutral person or body, as Paul and Barnabas took their case to the apostles in Jerusalem (Acts 15:1-2). The fifth is divine intervention, since there is a spiritual dimension to conflicts; the Council at Jerusalem resolved the crisis that would have permanently divided the church into Jews and Gentiles (Acts 15:23-29).

topic: The Biblical Basis of Human Rights
question: Write brief notes on the following terms: i. Human Dignity. ii. Human Equality. iii. Human Responsibility.
idealAnswer: John Stott holds that the origin of human rights is creation: we have never acquired them, no government has conferred them, we received them with our life from our Maker, and they are inherent in our creation. On that foundation he hinges the Biblical basis of human rights on three words — dignity, equality and responsibility. Human dignity rests on Genesis 1:27-28, where three issues stand out. Our relationship to God: God created man in his own image, so human beings have dignity as God-like beings, the divine image including those rational, moral and spiritual qualities which separate us from the animals and relate us to God. Our relationship to one another: male and female he created them, so that sexuality is God's creation, marriage his institution and human companionship his purpose, and whoever abuses these abuses God. Our relationship to the earth and its creatures: we are told to fill the earth and subdue it, and from this dominion flow the rights to work and to rest, to share in the earth's resources, to food, clothing and shelter, to life and health, and freedom from poverty, hunger and disease. Christians can also speak of a surpassing dignity derived from our Creator redeeming and recreating us through the incarnation and atonement of his Son. Human equality follows: the tragedy, Stott says, is that human rights have not always meant equal rights, for the good gifts of the Creator are spoiled by human selfishness, and the rights God gave to all equally degenerate into my rights on which I insist. The God we worship shows no partiality, so we must show none; Moses told Israel that the Lord shows no partiality and accepts no bribes, and Israelite judges were to do justice to the small and the great alike (Deut. 10:17-18). All human rights violations contradict the equality we enjoy by creation, for “He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker” (Prov. 14:31). Human responsibility is the last word derived from our createdness. Whenever human rights are emphasized to the exclusion of human responsibility we miss the Biblical pattern; discussions on rights often overlook the fact that human beings have duties as well as rights. The Bible calls us to defend other people's rights, but when it addresses us it emphasizes our responsibilities: our responsibility is to secure the other person's rights, forgoing our own in order to do so. Jesus Christ is the supreme model of this renunciation of rights (Phil. 2:6-7), and Paul, who had rights as an apostle, renounced them for the sake of the Gospel (1 Cor. 9).

Responsibility: the Bible emphasizes our duties, and calls us to secure others’ rights and forgo our own

question: (a) Define the term 'marriage'. (b) Discuss five challenges that confront married couples and suggest one way of solving each of the challenges identified.
idealAnswer: From the beginning the Bible presents marriage as a permanent, intimate union between a husband and wife, and Malachi's “I hate divorce” affirms that position; God's purpose is that the two become one, so that Jesus declared, “What God has joined together, let man not separate” (Matt. 19:6). The purpose for which it is entered is companionship (Gen. 2:18-24), and it is not to be entered for other reasons such as having children, money, status, satisfying sexual drive, pleasing parents and friends, independence from parents or an opportunity to travel abroad. Every marriage faces challenges, and a successful marriage results only when a couple learns to meet them. Financial strain arises when there is no money for the basic needs of the family; one does not have to be rich, but a couple must combine proper financial planning before and after the wedding with hard work and a lifestyle that suits their pocket, trusting God to give them the ability to create wealth (Deut. 8:18; 1 Tim. 5:8). Childlessness is a heavy burden in cultures where childbearing is regarded as the principal reason for marriage, and brings depression, disappointment, anxiety, anger and a feeling of sexual inadequacy; the couple should seek medical guidance and appropriate marriage counselling, show solidarity with each other in keeping their vows, and then trust God and leave the matter to his sovereign will. Sexual unfulfilment arises when one partner feels not sufficiently catered for sexually, from differences in libido, misinformation about sex, harmful cultural values, pornography, busy lifestyles, illness or psychological blocks, and it lowers self-esteem and may lead to alternative sexual activities and eventually to separation or divorce; couples need to seek solutions to the basic causes with competent professionals. Failure to keep the romance alive is another challenge, since relationships are nurtured by romance; the key is continuing with those practices that attracted the partners to each other before marriage, making time for each other and taking to hobbies and pastimes they enjoy. My children versus my spouse disrupts harmony when more attention is given to the children at the expense of the spouse and spouses take sides with the children as Isaac and Rebecca did; the couple must remember that the union before the altar was between husband and wife and must not allow that challenge to disrupt it. Other challenges the syllabus lists are transparency in times of prosperity, my spouse versus my career, long absence through travel abroad, “the little foxes” and demonic influences, against which the couple's greatest weapon is sharing their spiritual lives, studying God's word and praying together.

Childlessness — solved by medical guidance, counselling, solidarity and trust in God
Sexual unfulfilment — solved by addressing the basic causes with competent professionals
Keeping the romance alive — solved by making time and continuing pre-marital practices
My children versus my spouse — solved by remembering the union was between husband and wife

idealAnswer: Democracy is by far the most politically friendly of all political ideologies of the state as far as the Church is concerned, yet, as Winston Churchill remarked, it is the worst form of government except for all the others. Just as the Church needs democracy for the smooth operation of her mission, democracy needs the Church to overcome or minimize its inherent weaknesses. Against the tyranny of democracy — the tendency of politicians to serve the majority while neglecting or abusing the rights of the minority — the Church can help ensure that the government is fair to all its constituents and that minority rights and interests are protected as far as possible. Against the fallacy of democracy — defending the tyranny of the majority on the ground that democracy is by definition majority rule — the Church can expose this conceptual error and ensure that the government is non-discriminatory and fair to all citizens irrespective of political affiliation, race, ethnicity, age or sex, as Paul teaches in Galatians 3:28. Against the disease of democracy — electing representatives who make wonderful promises, fail, and attend to the people only when re-election approaches — the Church should educate her members and others on this selfish tendency and to study candidates well before voting, and should train and encourage altruistic, mature and otherwise qualified Christians to stand for office. Against red tapeism the Church can advise members in administration to minimize delays and to work as though they are working for God, and, for delays in the courts, can organize experienced church leaders, superannuated clergy, lawyers and retired judges into “Christian Family Arbitration Centres” to settle cases out of court. Where democracy acts as a catalyst for ethnic conflicts the churches in conflict-prone areas must be part of the early warning system, keep security agents informed, educate members and non-members on the dangers of ethnic conflict, preach against it and counsel those concerned. Against the problem of vagueness in such terms as freedom, justice, equality and peace, the Church can sensitize people to the ambiguities inherent in these terms and to how they can be manipulated by political adventurers and opposition parties. Against vulnerability to military coups, whose common cause is corruption, the Church, through her military chaplains, guest preachers to the barracks and the mass media, should help all to realize that corruption is part of human nature and cannot be removed by coups, and to appreciate the checks and balances of democracy and the power of the ballot box. In addition the Church prays for the state and supplements the government's efforts by establishing schools, vocational and technical institutes and agricultural research centres.
keyPoints: Democracy is the most politically friendly ideology for the Church, but is not perfect
Tyranny of democracy — the Church ensures fairness and the protection of minority rights
Fallacy of democracy — the Church exposes the conceptual error; Gal. 3:28
Disease of democracy — the Church educates voters and trains altruistic Christian candidates
Red tapeism — the Church urges minimal delays and sets up Christian Family Arbitration Centres
Catalyst for ethnic conflicts — the Church joins the early warning system and preaches against conflict
Problem of vagueness — the Church sensitizes people to ambiguous political terms
Vulnerability to military coups — the Church teaches that coups cannot remove corruption
The Church prays for the state and supplements its efforts in education and agriculture

subject: CS
topic: What does the Law in Ghana say about Homosexuality?
question: (a) Homosexuality is prohibited in the laws of Ghana; what does the law say? (b) Write notes on the various forms in which homosexuality is practised in Ghana.
idealAnswer: The law in Ghana regards homosexual intercourse as unnatural carnal knowledge and therefore illegal, and this is the reason the government disallowed the international conference of homosexuals that was planned to take place in Ghana in 2007. In traditional Ghanaian societies homosexual activity is a taboo, and in some societies the practice was so inconceivable that there were no words for it; Prof. K. A. Busia's doctoral research among the Asante in 1951, which discusses various sexual prohibitions, does not show the existence of homosexuality in the society at that time. As to the forms the practice takes, the syllabus describes three. The first is lesbianism in schools. Public knowledge of the female form of homosexuality limited it to the practice of supi in the boarding system of high schools, whereby some girls take other girls as sexual partners and engage in sexual activities in “tents” — student beds covered by bed sheets; in most cases senior girls take advantage of innocent fresh students, and there are stories of junior students bullied into such relationships. Some lesbian relationships involve female tutors and female students, and the syllabus recounts the case of a student in a female church institution whose long affair with a foreign member of staff left her emotionally devastated and eventually mentally ill when the woman left the country. The second is sodomy, the male form, which until recent times was prevalent among prison inmates; compared with supi among girls, the incidence of sodomy in boys' schools has been far less. Thus until recently homosexuality in Ghana was associated with institutional life, in prisons and schools, but today it has spread outside the institutions to hotels, guest houses, student hostels and private homes, and although the practice is outlawed, youth and adults of both sexes are involved in it for carnal pleasure and for money, with same-sex prostitution and partnerships gaining root underground. The third is sex tourism: some tourists visit the country for sexual adventures which include homosexual practices, and young people have been lured into same-sex prostitution by the attractive cash payments, as in the reported case of local boys photographed by European tourists whose parcel of photographs was intercepted by customs officers at the Post Office. Homosexual marriages are still unknown in Ghana because of the law, though in the name of human rights the international gay movement would join with local counterparts underground to lobby for recognition; South Africa is perhaps the only country in Africa that now permits same-sex marriages.

Sodomy — the male form, formerly prevalent among prison inmates, far less common in boys’ schools

subject: CS
question: (a) "Human beings are part of larger social groups called societies". Define the term Society. (b) Write an essay on the essential characteristics of a society.
idealAnswer: A Society is a group of people who conceive of themselves as distinct from other groups and who are connected together through communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics. What makes human societies different from groups of other social animals is that the members of human societies share a sense of common identity that grows out of their shared culture. More fully, Society may be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good; it is not a physical thing, for the only thing physical about Society is the members and their action. The essential characteristics follow from that definition. First, there can be no existing Society without members, and only rational and free beings can form a Society, since it is a union based on agreement about goals. Secondly, the members must be united in a stable or enduring way, so that a passing gathering is not a society. Thirdly, the members must cooperate or work together for the attainment of some end, and this end will be some common good that all the members will share and that no member could accomplish singly. Fourthly, Society is held together by bonds, moral bonds of means and ends: either the members bind themselves by contract, pledge or agreement, or the bonds are imposed upon them by some law, natural or positive. It is this moral bond that distinguishes a Society from a crowd, which makes the individuals committed members and obliges them to their commitment. Finally, to guide the cooperative effort to the common good, Society must be equipped with that moral power called authority, authority being the right to determine the means and direct the members in their use.

The members must cooperate for a common good no member could accomplish singly
Moral bonds — contract, pledge or agreement, or law — distinguish a Society from a crowd
Authority: the moral power to determine the means and direct the members in their use
Society is an enduring union of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good

subject: CS
question: (a) Define democracy as given by Abraham Lincoln. (b) Write notes on the following weaknesses of democracy and the Church’s response to them: (i) Catalyst for Ethnic Conflict. (ii) The Problem of Vagueness. (iii) Vulnerability to Military Coups. (iv) Fallacy of Democracy.
idealAnswer: As Abraham Lincoln beautifully expressed it, democracy is the government by the people, for the people and of the people. Being a government by the people means it is not imposed by anyone but chosen by the people themselves through elections under the guidance of a self-chosen constitution; being for the people means it ensures that the goods, services and protection offered by the state are as fairly distributed as possible to the benefit of all; and being of the people means that all sections of the populace — men, women, racial or ethnic minorities, rich or poor — are given equal opportunities to compete for political and administrative positions in the government. Democracy is nonetheless imperfect, and the syllabus notes several weaknesses. Democracy can be a catalyst for ethnic conflicts: recent history in eastern Europe, Africa and other emerging democracies shows a high correlation between democratization and the spread of ethnic conflict, since previously oppressed ethnic groups seize the opportunity afforded by the emphasis on freedom, human rights and in particular the right to self-determination, to separate themselves from their former oppressors. The Church's response is that churches in conflict-prone areas must be part of the early warning system and keep security agents informed of any attempt at separation or civil war, while educating members and non-members on the dangers of ethnic conflict, preaching against it and counselling those concerned. The problem of vagueness arises because the terms that constitute the tenets of democracy — freedom, justice, equality, democracy, peace, unity — are inherently vague and sometimes intolerably ambiguous, so that it is difficult to say when they have been achieved; one group may think enough peace and justice have been attained while another intensifies the struggle. The Church can sensitize people to these ambiguities, especially in the context of conflict resolution or prevention, and to how such terms can be manipulated by political adventurers and opposition parties. Vulnerability to military coups marks the democracies of post-colonial Africa and much of the Third World; Africa alone has witnessed about fifty coups, and without exception the common major cause cited is corruption, as in Nigeria and Sierra Leone. The Church, through her military chaplains, guest preachers to the barracks and the mass media, should help the military and all others to realize that corruption is part of human nature and cannot be removed by military coups, and to appreciate the checks and balances of democracy, strengthened by education and legislation and by the citizens' power to remove corrupt politicians through the ballot box without bloodshed. The fallacy of democracy is committed whenever one defends the tyranny of the majority by arguing that the practice is right since democracy is by definition the rule of the majority; this is a conceptual blunder, for majority rule does not and should not imply minority suffering, and democracy must promote freedom and justice for all. The Church can expose this conceptual error and ensure that the government is non-discriminatory and fair to all citizens irrespective of political affiliation, race, ethnicity, age or sex, as Paul says in Galatians 3:28 that there is no difference between Jew and Gentile, between men and women, for all are one in union with Christ Jesus.

"By the people" — chosen through elections under a self-chosen constitution
"For the people" — fair distribution of goods, services and protection
"Of the people" — equal opportunity for all sections of the populace
Catalyst for ethnic conflict — the Church joins the early warning system and preaches against conflict
Problem of vagueness — the Church sensitizes people to ambiguous political terms and their manipulation

subject: CS
question: (a) Define the term conflict. (b) As a Lay Preacher, identify five sources that can result in conflicts in the Church and give a suggested remedy for each.
idealAnswer: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship, whether at home, at work, in the church or in the nation: when people come together regularly, especially where issues of personal significance are involved, differences emerge, and those involved often become angry, hurt, bitter or defensive, so that a relationship may be damaged or ended. Conflict is not always destructive; it may be constructive, spotlighting problems that require attention and forcing the clarification of issues, and it is also experienced within ourselves as an inward struggle or restlessness of the soul. The syllabus identifies six common sources of conflict, of which five may be given. Differences in perception: no two individuals perceive things in the same way, which leads to misunderstanding, confusion and conflict; the remedy is honest communication, since silence and isolation deepen misunderstanding. Differences in priority or values: values are deeply held beliefs, and conflicts develop when people with different religious, moral, ideological or philosophical outlooks work together, and when values are at stake people find it hard to change their stand; the remedy is to get beneath surface issues and unseen motives so that the real disagreement is identified. Differences in expectations or role pressures: conflicts arise when expectations are not fulfilled, one party saying "I wanted you to…" and the other "I expected you to…"; the remedy is negotiation, a process of give and take in which neither party insists on being the winner. Divergent goals: members working for the same body but in different departments pursue different aims, which leads to competition for available resources and a lack of team effort; the remedy is negotiation and, where the parties cannot agree, external intervention by a neutral person or body, as Paul and Barnabas took their case to the apostles in Jerusalem. Self-esteem or status threat: where one person's self-esteem depends on having all the good ideas, and status and authority are involved, anger and frustration follow; and personality clashes, where troublesome individuals of hostile nature or of low self-esteem overcompensate by being belligerent. For these the remedy is divine intervention alongside the others, since there is a spiritual dimension to conflicts, and among believers Jesus' own procedure in Matthew 18:15-17 applies: approach the other party directly but privately, then seek two or three witnesses, then bring the matter to the church, and if the conflict persists treat the party who refuses reconciliation as an unbeliever.
keyPoints: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship — home, work, church, nation
Differences emerge when people come together regularly over issues of personal significance
Differences in perception — remedy: honest communication
Differences in priority or values — remedy: getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives
Differences in expectations or role pressures — remedy: negotiation
Divergent goals — remedy: negotiation and external intervention
Self-esteem or status threat — remedy: divine intervention and honest communication
Personality clashes — remedy: the steps of Matthew 18:15-17 among believers

topic: INTRODUCTION: THE NATURE OF HUMAN RIGHTS
question: (a) Outline the four (4) basic human needs according to Galting. (b) Write short notes on the following: (i) Materialism. (ii) Humanism. (iii) Secularism.
idealAnswer: One scholar suggests that the most fruitful way to think about human rights is to begin with the idea that ultimately they are supposed to serve basic human needs, and according to Galting (1994) the basic human needs which generate corresponding rights are four. Survival needs, to avoid violence: the right to be free from individual and collective violence. Well-being needs, to avoid misery: the right to adequate nutrition and water, to movement, sleep, sex and other biological wants, to protection from disease and from adverse climatological and environmental impacts. Identity needs, to avoid alienation: the right to self-expression, to realize one's potential, to establish and maintain emotional bonds with others, to preserve cultural heritage and association, to contribute through work and other activity, and to receive information about and maintain contact with nature, the global humanity and other aspects of the biosphere. Freedom needs, to avoid repression: the right to receive and express opinions, to assemble with others, to have a common policy, and to choose from a wide range in such matters as jobs, spouse, where to live and life style. Materialism is defined in the dictionary as the belief that only physical matter exists and the spiritual world does not, and such a believer is called a materialist; according to Yusufu Turaki, materialism is another form of secularism, whereby people's lives are dominated by their desire for worldly pleasures and bodily comforts and revolve around money, possessions and the things of this world. Humanism is a belief system based on the principle that people's spiritual and emotional needs can be fulfilled without following a god or religion, and such a believer is described as a humanist; secular humanism is likewise defined as a set of beliefs which emphasise the importance of reason and of individuals rather than religion. Secularism, as Turaki writes, threatens the deeply religious African approach to life, for it promotes a way of life and thought that is concerned only with this world and is opposed to thinking in terms of what is sacred or spiritual; it originated in Europe, in part as a reaction against the control of all areas of life by a church riddled with economic and political activities. B. J. Van der Walt calls secularism the mother of ideologies and the most dangerous enemy of Christianity, since it works unnoticed, gradually from the outside to the inside, and is a chameleon ideology, the medium for the growth of a variety of other ideologies.
keyPoints: Galting: survival needs — to avoid violence
Well-being needs — to avoid misery
Identity needs — to avoid alienation
Freedom needs — to avoid repression
Materialism: only physical matter exists and the spiritual world does not; lives dominated by worldly pleasures
Humanism: spiritual and emotional needs fulfilled without following a god or religion
Secularism: a way of life concerned only with this world, opposed to the sacred or spiritual
Secularism originated in Europe as a reaction against church control of all areas of life
Van der Walt: secularism is the "mother of ideologies" and the most dangerous enemy of Christianity

chapter: SEXUAL PERVERSION - WHAT IS THE BIBLICAL VIEW?
question: (a) Briefly define "Homosexuality". (b) Homosexual marriage is not Biblical. Highlight why you agree, with support from Scripture.
idealAnswer: Homosexuality is a term with two meanings: it may be applied to people who are sexually attracted to members of their own sex, or to same-sex genital acts, and it comprises both men and women, lesbianism being the word normally used to distinguish female homosexuality. A difference is to be noted between personal orientation and behaviour, for some people with a homosexual orientation never put their desires into practice, while others whose attraction is primarily heterosexual engage in homosexual acts occasionally; the syllabus notes that many experts agree that a homosexual orientation is discovered, not chosen. That homosexual marriage is not Biblical follows from the positive teaching of Genesis 1 and 2 about human sexuality and heterosexual marriage, in the light of which alone the Scriptural prohibitions make sense. Genesis 2 affirms the complementarity of the sexes, which constitutes the basis for heterosexual marriage: in Genesis 2:18 the human need for companionship is expressed — "It is not good for a man to be alone" — and God met that need by a special work of creation, making the woman out of the man and bringing her to him in a kind of divine marriage ceremony, so that Adam could say, "This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, for she was taken out of man." The concluding comment is Genesis 2:24: "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother, and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh." The image of woman, taken from man's flesh and becoming one flesh again with him in sexual union and marriage, is meaningless when applied to homosexual relationships; and homosexual expression, the syllabus says, endangers the formation of sexual identity in boys and girls, the integrity of the family and therefore the stability of the whole society. Jesus himself endorsed this Old Testament definition of marriage in Matthew 19:4-6, emphasizing its heterosexual nature with words from Genesis 1:27, that the Creator made them male and female; the three truths about marriage he affirmed are that heterosexual gender is a divine creation, that heterosexual marriage is a divine institution and that heterosexual fidelity is a divine intention, so that a homosexual affair is a breach of all three divine purposes. The Bible says nothing about the homosexual orientation but condemns homosexual behaviour forthrightly: Sodom suffered God's judgement for threatened homosexual rape (Gen. 19:1-25), the Holiness Code of Leviticus labelled male homosexuals detestable and prescribed the death penalty (Lev. 18:22; 20:13), and in the New Testament Paul condemns the practice as unnatural, incompatible with the lifestyle of God's kingdom and an affront to God's law and gospel (Rom. 1:18-27; 1 Cor. 6:9-11; 1 Tim. 1:8-11).

subject: CS
question: (a) What is marriage? (b) As a Lay Preacher, you have been tasked to counsel a newly married couple on challenges likely to confront their marriage. Outline four (4) of such challenges and suggest one remedy for each.
idealAnswer: From the beginning the Bible presents marriage as a permanent, intimate union between a husband and wife; God's purpose is that the two should become one, so that Jesus declared, "What God has joined together, let man not separate" (Matt. 19:6), and Malachi records the Lord's word, "I hate divorce". The purpose for which marriage is entered is companionship (Gen. 2:18-24), and it should not be entered for other reasons such as having children, money, enhancing status in society, satisfying sexual drive, pleasing parents and friends, being independent of parents or having an opportunity to travel abroad. Every marriage faces challenges, and a successful marriage results only when a couple learns to meet them. Financial strain arises where there is no money for the family's basic needs; one does not have to be rich, but the remedy is proper short- and long-term financial planning before and after the wedding, combined with hard work and a lifestyle that suits one's own pocket rather than following others, trusting God who gives the ability to create wealth (Deut. 8:18; 1 Tim. 5:8). Childlessness is a heavy burden where childbearing is regarded as the principal reason for marriage, and brings depression, disappointment, anxiety, shock, anger and a feeling of sexual inadequacy; the remedy is to seek solution through medical guidance and appropriate marriage counsellors, to show solidarity with each other in keeping the marriage vows, and then to trust God and leave the matter to his sovereign will, remembering that the godly offspring God desires does not involve biological children alone. Sexual unfulfilment arises when a partner feels not sufficiently catered for sexually, whether from differences in libido, misinformation about sex, harmful cultural values, pornography, busy lifestyles and stress, illness, or psychological blocks and sexual dysfunction; it lowers self-esteem and may lead to masturbation, pornography or extramarital affairs and eventually to separation or divorce, and the remedy is for the couple to seek solutions to the basic causes with competent professionals. Failure to keep the romance alive is a fourth challenge, for relationships are nurtured and nourished by romance, and neglecting it after marriage is like failing to nourish a child after birth; the remedy is to continue those practices that attracted the partners to each other before marriage, to make time for each other off their busy schedules and to take up hobbies and pastimes they enjoy together. Other challenges the couple should be warned of are children versus spouse, transparency in times of prosperity, spouse versus career, long absence through travel abroad, "the little foxes" and demonic influences, against which the couple's greatest weapon is sharing their spiritual lives, studying God's word and praying together.

Its purpose is companionship (Gen. 2:18-24)
Financial strain — remedy: planning, hard work, a lifestyle to suit one’s pocket, trust in God
Childlessness — remedy: medical guidance, counselling, solidarity, trust in God’s sovereign will
Sexual unfulfilment — remedy: seek the basic causes with competent professionals
Keeping the romance alive — remedy: time for each other and the practices of the courtship
Children versus spouse — remedy: remember the union was between husband and wife
Travel abroad, career, "the little foxes", demonic influences — remedy: shared spiritual life, study and prayer

subject: CS
topic: The Position of the Methodist Church Ghana
question: (a) What is divorce in marriage? (b) Outline what the Church’s Constitution says concerning divorce, dissolution of marriage and remarriage.
idealAnswer: Divorce is the dissolution of a marriage, the breaking of what the Bible presents from the beginning as a permanent, intimate union between a husband and wife. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 speaks of a man who marries a woman who becomes displeasing to him because he finds something indecent about her and who writes her a certificate of divorce, giving the man the right to decide whether a marriage shall continue or break; but Malachi records the Lord's own position, "I hate divorce", and Jesus went back to God's purpose in instituting marriage and declared, "What God has joined together, let man not separate" (Matt. 19:6), allowing divorce only on the ground of marital unfaithfulness, while Paul added the case of an unbelieving partner who breaks the marriage because of the believer's faith in Christ, on the basis that God has called us to live in peace (1 Cor. 7:15). The position of the Methodist Church Ghana is set out in Standing Order 743 of the Constitution, under the title Divorce, Dissolution of Marriage and Remarriage. First, no member of the Church shall dissolve his or her marriage without first consulting his or her Minister, who shall make every effort to reconcile the parties and shall, if need be, seek the assistance of the Leaders' Meeting. Secondly, if one partner fails in fulfilling the obligations of marriage, it is the duty of the other, as a Christian, to be active in seeking reconciliation so long as any possibility of it remains. Thirdly, where all efforts to effect reconciliation fail, the Leaders' Meeting shall be informed of this. Fourthly, when one party has already formed a union with a third person and is judged to be beyond hope of restoration to the lawful partner, the latter may be permitted to dissolve the marriage by the appropriate process under the Ordinance or Customary Law, and shall then be free to re-marry in due course; this permission to divorce and re-marry is subject to confirmation by the Bishop of the Diocese, acting in consultation with the Circuit Superintendent concerned and a small committee, including a lawyer, appointed by Synod. Finally, any member who dissolves his or her marriage against the advice of the Minister and the Leaders' Meeting, or who is the guilty party in divorce proceedings, or who contravenes S.O. 742 (3) (1), shall be subject to the discipline of the Leaders' Meeting.

subject: CS
question: (a) Define society. (b) Outline four (4) reasons why humans cannot live a life of solitude.
idealAnswer: A Society is a group of people who conceive of themselves as distinct from other groups and who are connected together through communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics; what makes human societies different from groups of other social animals is that their members share a sense of common identity that grows out of their shared culture. Society may also be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good, and it is not a physical thing, the only physical thing about it being the members and their action. Human beings are social animals: we live in communities that may be part of larger social groups called societies, and being born into and living with our family, race and nation is a fact of our human existence. Four reasons may be given why we cannot live a life of solitude. First, people abhor solitude and crave companionship: we spontaneously seek others and enjoy their company, whereas loneliness sets up a veritable hunger in the soul. Secondly, we cannot take care of ourselves alone: the child must be reared by the parents for many years, without the family no children grow up, and living in the family implies cooperation right from the beginning of each one's life. Thirdly, the gift of language fits us to communicate with one another, to discuss projects of common interest and to agree on means and ends for cooperative effort, so that the very ability of speech indicates that we are meant to live a social life. Fourthly, intellectual and moral development requires the constant communication of ideas and values among people, an exchange possible only in a Society. Society is therefore essential to humans, and Aristotle is right in saying that "the life of solitude is fit only for a beast or a god".

Members share a sense of common identity growing out of a shared culture

We cannot take care of ourselves alone; the child must be reared by parents
The gift of language fits us to communicate and to cooperate
Intellectual and moral development requires the exchange of ideas and values

subject: CS
question: (a) Define democracy. (b) What do you understand by the following weaknesses of democracy and the Church’s response to them? i. Tyranny of Democracy. ii. Fallacy of Democracy. iii. The Disease of Democracy. iv. Red Tapeism.
idealAnswer: Democracy, as Abraham Lincoln beautifully expressed it, is the government by the people, for the people and of the people. Being a government by the people means it is not imposed by anyone but chosen by the people themselves through elections under the guidance of a self-chosen constitution; being for the people means the goods, services and protection offered by the state are as fairly distributed as possible for the benefit of all; and being of the people means that all sections of the populace — men, women, racial or ethnic minorities, rich or poor — are given equal opportunities to compete for political and administrative positions. Democracy is the most politically friendly of all political ideologies as far as the Church is concerned, yet, as Churchill said, it is the worst form of government except for all the others. The tyranny of democracy is the tendency of politicians in a democracy to look out for the interest of the majority while neglecting the interest or abusing the rights of the minority, which is very dangerous where the majority happens to be of a particular racial, ethnic, religious or ideological orientation; the Church can help ensure that the government is fair to all its constituents and that minority rights and interests are protected as much as possible. The fallacy of democracy is committed whenever one tries to defend the tyranny of the majority by arguing that the practice is right since democracy is by definition the rule of the majority; it is a conceptual blunder, for majority rule does not and should not imply minority suffering, and democracy must promote freedom and justice for all. The Church can expose this conceptual error and ensure that the government is non-discriminatory but fair to all citizens irrespective of political affiliation, race, ethnicity, age or sex, which is supported by Paul's statement in Galatians 3:28 that there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles, between men and women, for all are one in union with Christ Jesus. The disease of democracy is the taunt of socialist critics that democracy is sick of an incurable disease, namely the frequent election of representatives who make wonderful promises to help their constituents, fail to do so, and attempt to help the people only when they need to seek re-election amid tough competition; the Church should educate her members and others on this selfish tendency and on studying candidates well before voting, and should train and encourage non-selfish, altruistic and mature Christians who are otherwise qualified to stand for office. Red tapeism is the tendency to complicate and unduly delay administrative and legal procedures so much that those at the receiving end feel frustrated and unsatisfied or that justice has been denied them, so that they may be tempted to bribe their way out — which breeds more corruption — or to take the law into their own hands; the Church can advise its members in administration to minimize delays and to work as if they are working for God, and, for delays in the courts, can organize experienced church leaders, superannuated clergy, lawyers and retired judges and magistrates into "Christian Family Arbitration Centres" for conflict resolution, to help settle cases out of court and decongest the overburdened legal system.

question: (a) What do you understand by the term conflict? (b) Outline five (5) principles of conflict resolution according to Tokunboh Adeyemo.
idealAnswer: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship, whether at home, at work, in the church or in the nation. When people come together regularly, especially when issues of personal significance are involved, differences emerge; and when conflict occurs between people, individually or in groups, they often become angry, hurt, bitter or defensive, so that the conflict sometimes ends a relationship or seriously damages it. Yet conflict is inevitable and can have either constructive or destructive results: conflicts sometimes measure the health of an organization, since groups in which nothing happens important enough to make people fight have a greater chance of dying than groups where dissension occurs; conflicts spotlight problems that require attention; and conflicts may force clarification of issues and challenge leaders to question the status quo and search for better solutions, as the good handling of the conflict between the Greeks and the Jews in the Early Church in Jerusalem resulted in the rapid growth of the Church (Acts 6:1-7). We also experience conflict within ourselves, in an inward personal struggle or restlessness of the soul. In his article in the Africa Bible Commentary, Tokunboh Adeyemo writes that when we manage a conflict we simply organize, regulate and take charge of it in order to make it serve a good cause, and that in resolving any conflict there are three key questions to ask: what are we agreeing or disagreeing about; why are we agreeing or disagreeing; and how can we get past this and move forward? He proposes five principles to guide us. Honest communication: silence and isolation deepen misunderstanding, which fuels conflict, so that Abraham did not gloss over the potential for quarrels between his herdsmen and Lot's but discussed it openly and developed an appropriate strategy (Gen. 13:1-18). Getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives: often the apparent cause of a conflict is not the real issue, which is rooted in people's underlying motives and beliefs, as the real problem between the people of Gerar and Isaac went beyond water (Gen. 26:19-31). Negotiation: the best way to find peace is through a process of give and take in which neither party insists on being the winner, and the story of 1 Kings 12 shows the disastrous consequence of Rehoboam's unwillingness to negotiate. External intervention: the parties may be so caught up in the conflict that they cannot talk to one another, so that the assistance of a neutral person such as a marriage counsellor, or an organization like the United Nations, may be sought, as Paul and Barnabas and their opponents took their case to the apostles in Jerusalem (Acts 15:1-2). Divine intervention: there is a spiritual dimension to conflicts, so in resolving them we need to seek divine assistance, and it was the Council at Jerusalem that resolved the crisis which would have permanently divided the church into Jews and Gentiles (Acts 15:23-29).
keyPoints: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship
It can have constructive or destructive results and may measure the health of an organization

question: (a) Define the term marriage. (b) Write full notes on the following challenges in marriage: i. Financial strain. ii. Childlessness. iii. The little Foxes. iv. Keeping the Romance Alive. v. My child versus my spouse.
idealAnswer: From the beginning the Bible presents marriage as a permanent, intimate union between a husband and wife, so that God's purpose is that the two should become one and Jesus declared, "What God has joined together, let man not separate" (Matt. 19:6); its purpose is companionship (Gen. 2:18-24), and it should not be entered into for any other reason. Financial strain: one does not have to be rich to have a successful marriage, but when there is a lack of money to take care of the family's basic needs it puts a strain on the relationship, for "If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for his immediate family, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever" (1 Tim. 5:8). Some couples plunge into this problem just after the wedding because they failed to do proper short- and long-term financial planning beforehand; it can be overcome only by combining proper planning, hard work and a lifestyle which suits one's own pocket instead of following what others do, learning from the beginning to be faithful to God in these matters and trusting him to give the ability to create wealth (Deut. 8:18). Childlessness poses a big challenge in cultures such as ours, for which childbearing is the principal reason for marriage; in most cases the woman is falsely accused of being barren and relatives, especially from the man's family, demand an offspring, and the results are depression, disappointment, anxiety, shock, anger and such emotional reactions as a feeling of sexual inadequacy and failure. Since the reasons may be infertility, miscarriage or the loss of a child shortly after birth, the couple should seek solution through medical guidance and appropriate marriage counsellors, show solidarity with each other in their vows to be faithful till death, and then trust God and leave everything to his sovereign will, noting that the godly offspring God desires does not involve biological children alone (Mal. 2:15). "The little foxes" is the phrase from Song of Songs 2:15 — "Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, our vineyards that are in bloom" — by which Solomon describes the issues that disturb the peace of a marriage: matters that appear minor to an outsider but have the potential of disturbing a marriage to the point of divorce, such as how differences of temperament are handled, dealings with in-laws, communication and similar issues. These foxes will always be around, especially as a newly-wed couple gets to know each other, and the important thing is not to allow them to frustrate us and take away our peace. Keeping the romance alive is neglected by most couples after marriage, though relationships are nurtured and nourished by romance leading to wedlock; failure to keep it alive is like failing to nourish the child after birth, and will automatically lead to "Kwashiorkor". It demands that the couple have time for each other, and it becomes difficult as the marriage ages, especially where the choice of partner was blinded by infatuation and sexual attraction rather than true and sincere love; the key is continuing with those practices that attracted one to the other during the pre-marital relationship, taking up hobbies and pastimes they enjoy and finding time off their busy schedules, for by inspiring the most romantic book in the world, the Song of Solomon, God teaches us to keep romance alive in marriage. My children versus my spouse: sharing time and attention between spouse and children can disrupt marital harmony, especially after the first child is born, when more attention is given to the children at the expense of the spouse; the strain becomes intense and destructive when spouses take sides with the children, as happened with Isaac and Rebecca over Jacob and Esau. The couple must note that the union before the altar was between husband and wife, excluding the children, who will in future be united to their own partners, and the challenge is especially intense where a spouse already has children from a previous relationship.

Keeping the romance alive — neglect is like failing to nourish a child; make time and continue courtship practices

topic: The Biblical Basis of Human Rights
question: (a) Mention the four (4) basic human needs according to Galting. (b) Write brief notes on each of the following terms: i. Human Dignity. ii. Human Equality. iii. Human Responsibility.
idealAnswer: According to Galting (1994) the basic human needs which generate corresponding rights are four. Survival needs, to avoid violence: the right to be free from individual and collective violence. Well-being needs, to avoid misery: the right to adequate nutrition and water, to movement, sleep, sex and other biological wants, and to protection from disease and adverse climatological and environmental impacts. Identity needs, to avoid alienation: the right to self-expression, to realize one's potential, to establish and maintain emotional bonds with others, to preserve cultural heritage and association, to contribute through work, and to receive information about and maintain contact with nature and the global humanity. Freedom needs, to avoid repression: the right to receive and express opinions, to assemble with others, to have a common policy, and to choose from a wide range in such matters as jobs, spouse, where to live and life style. John Stott holds that the origin of human rights is creation, that we never acquired them and no government conferred them, and he hinges their Biblical basis on three words — dignity, equality and responsibility. Human dignity is based on Genesis 1:27-28, where three issues stand out: our relationship to God, since God created man in his own image, the divine image including those rational, moral and spiritual qualities which separate us from the animals and relate us to God; our relationship to one another, since male and female he created them, so that sexuality is God's creation, marriage his institution and human companionship his purpose, and whoever abuses these abuses God; and our relationship to the earth and its creatures, since God has given us dominion with instructions to subdue and cultivate the earth, from which flow the rights to work and to rest, to share in the earth's resources, to food, clothing and shelter, to life and health, and freedom from poverty, hunger and disease. Christians may add the surpassing dignity derived from our Creator redeeming and recreating us through the incarnation and atonement of his Son. Human equality follows: the tragedy, Stott says, is that human rights have not always meant equal rights, since the good gifts of the Creator are spoiled by human selfishness and the rights God gave to all equally degenerate into my rights on which I insist. The God we worship shows no partiality, so we must show none and give no special deference to the rich, famous or influential; Moses told Israel that the Lord shows no partiality and accepts no bribes, and Israelite judges were to do justice to the small and to the great alike (Deut. 10:17-18). All human rights violations contradict the equality we enjoy by creation, for "He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker" (Prov. 14:31). Human responsibility is the last word derived from our createdness: whenever human rights are emphasized to the exclusion of human responsibility we miss the Biblical pattern, and discussions of rights often overlook the fact that human beings have duties as well as rights. The Bible calls us to defend other people's rights, but when it addresses us it emphasizes our responsibilities: to secure the other person's rights, forgoing our own in order to do so. Jesus Christ is the supreme model of this renunciation of rights (Phil. 2:6-7), and Paul, who had rights as an apostle, renounced them for the sake of the Gospel to become everybody's slave and serve their rights (1 Cor. 9).
keyPoints: Galting: survival needs (to avoid violence), well-being needs (to avoid misery), identity needs (to avoid alienation), freedom needs (to avoid repression)

Dignity from Gen. 1:27-28 — relationship to God, to one another, and to the earth and its creatures
The divine image includes rational, moral and spiritual qualities
Equality: God shows no partiality, so neither may we (Deut. 10:17-18; Prov. 14:31)
Human rights violations contradict the equality we enjoy by creation
Responsibility: we have duties as well as rights, and must secure others’ rights and forgo our own
Christ (Phil. 2:6-7) and Paul (1 Cor. 9) as models of renouncing rights

question: (a) Briefly state what the Law in Ghana says about Homosexuality. (b) Write briefly on the practices of Homosexuality in Ghana under the following headings: i. Lesbianism in Schools. ii. Sodomy. iii. Sex Tourism.
idealAnswer: The law in Ghana regards homosexual intercourse as unnatural carnal knowledge and therefore illegal, and it is for this reason that the government disallowed the international conference of homosexuals that was planned to take place in Ghana in 2007. In traditional Ghanaian societies homosexual activity is a taboo, and in some societies the practice was so inconceivable that there were no words for it; Prof. K. A. Busia's doctoral research among the Asante in 1951, which discusses various sexual prohibitions, does not show the existence of homosexuality in that society at the time. Lesbianism in schools: public knowledge of the female form of homosexuality limited it to the practice of supi in the boarding system of high schools, the system whereby some girls take other girls in the school as sexual partners and engage in sexual activities in "tents", that is, student beds covered by bed sheets. In most cases the senior girls take advantage of the innocent fresh students to satisfy their sexual lusts, and there are stories of junior students bullied into the relationship by some seniors. Some lesbian relationships involve female tutors and female students; the syllabus recounts the case of a student in a female church institution who was involved with a foreign woman on the staff, an affair which lasted long after the student had graduated and left her emotionally devastated and eventually mentally ill when the woman left the country. Sodomy: until recent times the male form, sodomy, was prevalent among prison inmates, and compared with the supi among girls the incidence of sodomy in boys' schools has been far less. Thus until recently homosexuality in Ghana was associated with institutional life, in prisons and schools; today the story is different, for homosexuality has spread outside the institutions to hotels, guest houses, student hostels and private homes, and although the practice is outlawed, youth and adults of both sexes are involved in it for carnal pleasure and for money, so that same-sex prostitution and partnerships are gaining root underground. Sex tourism: an important factor for the growth of homosexual activity in Ghana is sex tourism, some tourists visiting the country for sexual adventures which include homosexual practices, and young people have been lured to become same-sex prostitutes because of the attractive cash payments involved. The syllabus reports an incident involving some local boys and European tourists who photographed their encounters and later posted printed copies to the boys; customs officers at the parcel section of the Post Office inspected the contents, and the boy who went to collect the parcel was arrested and handed over to the police. Homosexual marriages are still unknown in Ghana because of the law, though in the name of human rights the international gay movement would join hands with local counterparts underground to lobby for recognition; South Africa is perhaps the only country in Africa that now permits same-sex marriages.
keyPoints: Ghanaian law regards homosexual intercourse as unnatural carnal knowledge and therefore illegal
The planned international conference of homosexuals was disallowed in 2007
Traditional Ghanaian societies treat the practice as a taboo; Busia’s 1951 Asante research found no evidence of it
Lesbianism in schools — supi in the boarding system, sexual activity in "tents"
Seniors take advantage of, and sometimes bully, juniors; some cases involve female tutors
Sodomy — the male form, prevalent among prison inmates, far less common in boys’ schools
The practice has spread from institutions to hotels, guest houses, hostels and private homes
Sex tourism — tourists visiting for sexual adventures; young people lured by cash payments

subject: CS
topic: The Position of the Methodist Church Ghana
question: (a) Define divorce. (b) What is the position of the Methodist Church Ghana on Divorce, Dissolution of Marriage and Remarriage as enshrined in S.O. 743 of the Constitution?
idealAnswer: Divorce is the dissolution of a marriage, the breaking of what the Bible presents from the beginning as a permanent, intimate union between a husband and wife. Deuteronomy 24:1-4 allows a man who finds something indecent about his wife to write her a certificate of divorce, giving the man the right to decide whether a marriage shall continue or break; but the Lord's own position, declared through Malachi, is "I hate divorce", and Jesus went back to God's purpose in instituting marriage and declared, "What God has joined together, let man not separate" (Matt. 19:6), allowing divorce only on the ground of marital unfaithfulness, while Paul added the exceptional case of an unbelieving partner who breaks the marriage because of the believer's faith in Christ, on the basis that God has called us to live in peace (1 Cor. 7:15). The Church's position is found in Standing Order 743 of the Constitution, under the title Divorce, Dissolution of Marriage and Remarriage. First, no member of the Church shall dissolve his or her marriage without first consulting his or her Minister, who shall make every effort to reconcile the parties and shall, if need be, seek the assistance of the Leaders' Meeting. Secondly, if one partner fails in fulfilling the obligations of marriage, it is the duty of the other, as a Christian, to be active in seeking reconciliation so long as any possibility of it remains. Thirdly, where all efforts to effect reconciliation fail, the Leaders' Meeting shall be informed of this. Fourthly, when one party has already formed a union with a third person and is judged to be beyond hope of restoration to the lawful partner, the latter may be permitted to dissolve the marriage by the appropriate process under the Ordinance or Customary Law, and shall then be free to re-marry in due course; this permission to divorce and re-marry is subject to confirmation by the Bishop of the Diocese, who shall act in consultation with the Circuit Superintendent concerned and a small committee, including a lawyer, appointed by Synod. Finally, any member who dissolves his or her marriage against the advice of the Minister and the Leaders' Meeting, or who is the guilty party in divorce proceedings, or who contravenes S.O. 742 (3) (1), shall be subject to the discipline of the Leaders' Meeting. The syllabus adds that the "peace" or "freedom" principle established by Paul may be extended to other cases after all efforts have been made to save a marriage, and that this appears to be the spirit of S.O. 743.

S.O. 743 (iii): where all efforts fail, the Leaders’ Meeting is informed
S.O. 743 (iv): where one party has formed a union with a third person and is beyond hope of restoration, the other may dissolve the marriage and re-marry
That permission is subject to confirmation by the Bishop of the Diocese, in consultation with the Circuit Superintendent and a committee including a lawyer
S.O. 743 (v): a member who divorces against advice, or is the guilty party, is subject to the discipline of the Leaders’ Meeting

subject: CS
question: (a) What do you understand by the term society? (b) Outline four essential characteristics of society.
idealAnswer: Human beings are social animals: we live in communities that may be part of larger social groups called societies, and a personal being is never an isolated being, for we find our primary experience to be that of living in relation with one another, sharing a whole set of values, perceptions, ideas and emotions. A Society, therefore, is a group of people who conceive of themselves as distinct from other groups and who are connected together through communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics; what makes human societies different from groups of other social animals is that their members share a sense of common identity that grows out of their shared culture. Society may also be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good; it is not a physical thing, the only thing physical about it being the members and their action. The essential characteristics are as follows. First, there can be no existing Society without members, and only rational and free beings can form a Society, since it is a union based on agreement about goals. Secondly, the members must be united in a stable or enduring way. Thirdly, the members must cooperate or work together for the attainment of some end, and this end will be some common good that all the members will share and that no member could accomplish singly. Fourthly, Society is held together by bonds, moral bonds of means and ends: either the members bind themselves by contract, pledge or agreement, or the bonds are imposed upon them by some law, natural or positive; and it is this moral bond that distinguishes a Society from a crowd, which makes the individuals committed members and obliges them to their commitment. To these may be added authority, that moral power with which Society must be equipped to guide the cooperative effort to the common good, authority being the right to determine the means and direct the members in their use.
keyPoints: Human beings are social animals living in communities that form larger groups called societies
A Society is a group of people distinct from other groups, connected by communication ties, customs and institutions
Members share a sense of common identity growing out of a shared culture
Members: only rational and free beings can form a Society
Stability: the members must be united in an enduring way
Cooperation for a common good no member could accomplish singly
Moral bonds — contract, pledge, agreement or law — distinguish a Society from a crowd
Authority: the moral power to determine the means and direct the members

question: Outline the four (4) basic human needs according to Galting.
idealAnswer: We are used to thinking about human rights in terms of freedom from specific abuses or restrictions, especially by governments, but there is a more comprehensive concept of rights, which holds that peoples and groups not only have the right not to be specifically abused but also have rights to a quality of life that at a minimum does not detract from their human dignity. One scholar suggests that the most fruitful way to think about human rights is to begin with the idea that ultimately they are supposed to serve basic human needs (Galting, 1994), and according to Galting the basic human needs which generate corresponding rights are four. Survival needs, to avoid violence: this is the right to be free from individual and collective violence. Well-being needs, to avoid misery: the right to adequate nutrition and water; to movement, sleep, sex and other biological wants; to protection from diseases and from adverse climatological and environmental impacts. Identity needs, to avoid alienation: the right to self-expression; to realize one's potential; to establish and maintain emotional bonds with others; to preserve cultural heritage and association; to contribute through work and other activity; and to receive information about and maintain contact with nature, the global humanity and other aspects of the biosphere. Freedom needs, to avoid repression: the right to receive and express opinions, to assemble with others, to have a common policy, and to choose from a wide range in such matters as jobs, spouse, where to live and life style.
keyPoints: Human rights are ultimately supposed to serve basic human needs (Galting, 1994)
Survival needs — to avoid violence: freedom from individual and collective violence
Well-being needs — to avoid misery: nutrition, water, movement, sleep, protection from disease
Identity needs — to avoid alienation: self-expression, potential, emotional bonds, cultural heritage
Freedom needs — to avoid repression: opinion, assembly, common policy, and choice of job, spouse and lifestyle

question: (a) Define the term 'democracy'. (b) Write notes on the following and suggest the Church's role in sustaining them: i. The Tyranny of Democracy. ii. Disease of Democracy. iii. Red Tapeism. iv. Catalyst for Ethnic Conflicts.
idealAnswer: Democracy, as Abraham Lincoln beautifully expressed it, is the government by the people, for the people and of the people: by the people, in that it is not imposed by anyone but chosen by the people themselves through elections under the guidance of a self-chosen constitution; for the people, in that it ensures that the goods, services and protection offered by the state are as fairly distributed as possible for the benefit of all; and of the people, in that all sections of the populace — men, women, racial or ethnic minorities, rich or poor — are given equal opportunities to compete for political and administrative positions. The tyranny of democracy is the tendency of politicians in a democracy to look out for the interest of the majority while neglecting the interest or abusing the rights of the minority, which can be very dangerous where the majority is of a particular racial, ethnic, religious or ideological orientation; the Church can help ensure that the government is fair to all its constituents and that minority rights and interests are protected as much as possible. The disease of democracy is what socialist critics call its incurable sickness, the frequent election of representatives who make wonderful promises to help their constituents, fail them, and attempt to help the people only when they need to seek re-election amid tough competition; the Church should educate her members and others on this selfish tendency and on studying political candidates very well before voting, and should train and encourage non-selfish, altruistic and mature Christians, otherwise qualified, to stand as candidates for office. Red tapeism is the tendency to complicate and unduly delay administrative and legal procedures so much that those at the receiving end feel frustrated and unsatisfied or that justice has been denied them, tempting them to bribe their way out, which breeds more corruption, or to despair of the courts and take the law into their own hands; the Church can advise its members in administration to minimize delays and to work as if they are working for God, and, for delays in the courts, can organize experienced church leaders, superannuated clergy, lawyers and retired judges and magistrates into "Christian Family Arbitration Centres" for conflict resolution, to settle cases out of court and help decongest the overburdened legal system. As a catalyst for ethnic conflicts, democracy shows in recent history in eastern Europe, Africa and other emerging democracies a high correlation between democratization and the spread of ethnic conflicts, since previously oppressed and exploited ethnic groups seize the opportunity afforded by the prevailing wind of change, with its emphasis on freedom, human rights and in particular the right to self-determination, to separate themselves from their former oppressors; churches in conflict-prone areas must be part of the early warning system, keeping security agents informed of any attempt at separation or civil war, while educating members and non-members on the dangers of ethnic conflicts, preaching against them and counselling those concerned against such destabilizing moves.
keyPoints: Lincoln: democracy is government by the people, for the people and of the people
Tyranny of democracy — serving the majority while neglecting or abusing minority rights
The Church ensures fairness to all constituents and protection of minority rights
Disease of democracy — representatives who promise, fail, and return only at re-election
The Church educates voters and trains altruistic Christian candidates
Red tapeism — undue delay in administrative and legal procedures, breeding bribery
The Church urges minimal delay and sets up Christian Family Arbitration Centres
Catalyst for ethnic conflicts — democratization correlates with ethnic conflict and self-determination claims
The Church joins the early warning system and preaches against ethnic conflict

subject: CS
question: (a) Define the term conflict. (b) As a Lay Preacher identify five common sources of conflict in the Society.
idealAnswer: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship, whether at home, at work, in the church or in the nation; when people come together regularly, especially when issues of personal significance are involved, differences emerge, and when conflict occurs between people, individually or in groups, they often become angry, hurt, bitter or defensive, so that the conflict sometimes ends a relationship or seriously damages it. Conflict is nevertheless inevitable and may have either constructive or destructive results: it sometimes measures the health of an organization, since groups in which nothing important enough happens to make people fight have a greater chance of dying than groups where dissension occurs; it spotlights problems that require attention; and it may force clarification of issues and challenge leaders to question the status quo and search for better solutions, as the good handling of the conflict between the Greeks and the Jews in the Early Church in Jerusalem resulted in the rapid growth of the Church. We also experience conflict within ourselves, in an inward personal struggle or restlessness of the soul. The syllabus identifies six common causes of conflict, of which five may be given. Differences in perception: no two individuals perceive things in the same way, and this often leads to misunderstanding, confusion and conflict. Differences in priority or values: values are deeply held beliefs, and conflicts often develop when people with different value systems try to work together, arising over differences in religious, moral, ideological or philosophical outlooks; when conflict concerns values people have difficulty in changing their stand. Differences in expectations or role pressures: conflicts often arise over different expectations when they are not fulfilled, one person saying "I wanted you to…" and the other replying "I expected you to…". Divergent goals: where two people work for the same organization but in different departments, one seeking greater profit by improving the quality of the products and the other by decreasing costs, competition among managers for available resources follows, and lack of team effort can develop into enormous conflict situations. Self-esteem or status threat: one person may have a good idea, but the other's self-esteem depends on his having all the good ideas, and where he is the boss and bosses know best, status and authority become sources of anger and frustration. Personality clashes: troublesome individuals have hostile natures and are predisposed toward conflict, people with strong needs to bully use their jobs to express hostility, and individuals with low self-esteem often overcompensate by being belligerent or hostile toward other people.
