chapter: RELIGIOUS PLURALISM AND THE CHRISTIAN MESSAGE
question: Write notes on the following: i. Materialism. ii. Humanism. iii. Secularism.
idealAnswer: The three "isms" deal with the same thing, and B. J. Van der Walt, in his book The Liberating Message — A Christian Worldview for Africa (1994), described secularism as the "mother of ideologies". Materialism is defined in the dictionary as the belief that only physical matter exists and the spiritual world does not, and such a believer is referred to as a materialist; according to Yusufu Turaki, materialism is another form of secularism, whereby people's lives are dominated by their desire for worldly pleasures and bodily comforts and revolve around money, possessions and the things of this world. Humanism is defined as a belief system based on the principle that people's spiritual and emotional needs can be fulfilled without following a god or religion, and such a believer is described as a humanist; secular humanism is likewise defined as a set of beliefs which emphasise the importance of reason and of individuals rather than religion. Secularism, as Yusufu Turaki writes in the Africa Bible Commentary, threatens the deeply religious African approach to all of life, for it is a Western philosophy which promotes a way of life and thought that is concerned only with this world and is opposed to thinking in terms of what is sacred or spiritual; it originated in Europe, in part as a reaction against the control of all areas of life by a church that was riddled with economic and political activities. Van der Walt observes that secularism did not intrude into Christianity from outside, for its germinating seed could already be discerned in the dualist Christianity of the Middle Ages, when the church began to distinguish between the natural and the supernatural, between aspects of life that involved God and those that did not; instead of the Christian conquering the world, the world has conquered the Christian. The process was gradual, taking three centuries from about the sixteenth century of the Renaissance and Humanism, but it has grown irresistibly, aided by the powers modern man has acquired — science, the power of knowledge; technology, the power of tools; and organization, the power of planning, integrating, co-ordinating and controlling — since modern man supposes that the greater his power, the less he needs God's help. Van der Walt calls secularism the most dangerous enemy of Christianity, because it is not an open enemy attacking with physical weaponry but works practically unnoticed, infiltrating and undermining faith; it works gradually from the outside to the inside, so that when we realize that an institution or the whole of life has been secularized it is already too late; and it is not a clearly discernible phenomenon but a chameleon ideology, the medium for the growth of a variety of other ideologies. The Bible's clear response to this way of life is found in Ecclesiastes, where Solomon on reflection found life to be "a chasing after the wind"; and Turaki advises that religion provides ethical and social values that affect people in their private and public lives and makes for responsible living, so that Christians must exhibit their Christian life (Matt. 5:13-16) in our secularized and materialistic societies in order to have influence.

Humanism: spiritual and emotional needs fulfilled without following a god or religion
Secular humanism emphasises reason and the individual rather than religion
Secularism: a way of life and thought concerned only with this world, opposed to the sacred or spiritual
It originated in Europe as a reaction against church control of all areas of life

It works unnoticed, gradually from outside to inside, and is a chameleon ideology
The Christian response: exhibit the Christian life (Matt. 5:13-16) in a secularized society

question: (a) What is marriage? (b) As a Lay Preacher, you have been tasked to exhort a newly married couple on challenges that are likely to be faced in their marriage. Outline four (4) of such challenges and suggest a remedy for each.
idealAnswer: From the beginning the Bible presents marriage as a permanent, intimate union between a husband and wife; God's purpose is that the two should become one, so Jesus declared, "What God has joined together, let man not separate" (Matt. 19:6). Its purpose is companionship (Gen. 2:18-24), and it should not be entered into for other reasons such as having children, money, enhancing status in society, satisfying sexual drive, pleasing parents and friends, being independent from parents or having an opportunity to travel abroad. Divorce is often the end result of a series of problems that a couple has failed to deal with successfully, and a successful marriage results only when a couple learns to meet the challenges it faces. Financial strain arises when there is a lack of money to take care of the family's basic needs; the remedy is proper short- and long-term financial planning, hard work and a lifestyle that suits one's own pocket instead of following what others do, learning from the beginning to be faithful to God and trusting him to give the ability to create wealth (Deut. 8:18; 1 Tim. 5:8). Childlessness is a heavy burden in cultures where childbearing is the principal reason for marriage, and brings depression, disappointment, anxiety, shock, anger and feelings of sexual inadequacy; the remedy is to seek solution through medical guidance and appropriate marriage counsellors, to show solidarity with each other in remembering the marriage vows, and then to trust God and leave everything to his sovereign will. Sexual unfulfilment arises when a partner feels not sufficiently catered for sexually, from differences in libido, misinformation about sex, harmful cultural values, pornography, busy lifestyles and stress, illness or psychological blocks; it lowers self-esteem and may lead to alternative sexual activities and eventually to separation or divorce, and the remedy is for the couple to seek solutions to the basic causes with competent professionals. Failure to keep the romance alive is a fourth challenge, since relationships are nurtured and nourished by romance and neglecting it is like failing to nourish a child after birth; the remedy is to have time for each other and to continue with those practices that attracted the partners to each other during the pre-marital relationship, taking up the hobbies and pastimes they enjoy. Other challenges to warn the couple of are my children versus my spouse, transparency in times of prosperity, my spouse versus my career, long absence through travel abroad, "the little foxes" and demonic influences; against these the couple's greatest weapon is in how they share their spiritual lives together, seeking the will of God through the study of his word and praying together, so building a strong fortress against the Enemy.

Its purpose is companionship (Gen. 2:18-24)
Financial strain — remedy: planning, hard work, a lifestyle to suit one’s pocket, trust in God
Childlessness — remedy: medical guidance, counselling, solidarity, trust in God’s sovereign will
Sexual unfulfilment — remedy: address the basic causes with competent professionals
Keeping the romance alive — remedy: time for each other and the practices of the courtship
Other challenges: children versus spouse, prosperity, career, travel abroad, "the little foxes", demonic influences
The couple’s greatest weapon is their shared spiritual life, study of the word and prayer

topic: Why Homosexual Marriage is not Biblical
question: (a) What is Homosexuality? (b) Write an essay on why homosexual marriage is not Biblical.
idealAnswer: Homosexuality is a term with two meanings: it may be applied to people who are sexually attracted to members of their own sex, or to same-sex genital acts, and it comprises both men and women, lesbianism being the word normally used to distinguish female homosexuality. A difference is to be noted between personal orientation and behaviour, for studies show that some people with a homosexual orientation never put their desires into practice, while others whose attraction is primarily heterosexual engage in homosexual acts occasionally; there is no consensus about the causation of same-sex desires, though many experts agree that a homosexual orientation is discovered, not chosen. That homosexual marriage is not Biblical follows from the positive teaching of Genesis 1 and 2 about human sexuality and heterosexual marriage, in the light of which alone the prohibitions of Scripture make sense. Genesis 2 particularly affirms the complementarity of the sexes, which constitutes the basis for heterosexual marriage: in Genesis 2:18 the human need for companionship is expressed — "It is not good for a man to be alone" — and Genesis 2 reveals the divine provision to meet that need, for a special work of divine creation took place in which God created the woman out of the man and brought her to him in a kind of divine marriage ceremony, so that Adam composed the first love poem in history: "This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, for she was taken out of man." The concluding comment is Genesis 2:24: "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother, and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh." The image of woman, taken from man's flesh and becoming one flesh again with him in sexual union and marriage, is meaningless when applied to homosexual relationships; and homosexual expression endangers the formation of sexual identity in boys and girls, the integrity of the family, and therefore the stability of the whole society. In Matthew 19:4-6 Jesus himself endorsed the Old Testament definition of marriage, emphasizing its heterosexual nature with words from Genesis 1:27, that the Creator made them male and female, and the three truths about marriage he affirmed are that heterosexual gender is a divine creation, that heterosexual marriage is a divine institution, and that heterosexual fidelity is a divine intention; a homosexual affair is a breach of all three of these divine purposes. An important facet of theology expressed by the ban on homosexual acts in the Old Testament law is the "one flesh" pattern of heterosexual marriage in Genesis, which is why Paul bracketed homosexual behaviour with adultery in his updated application of the Ten Commandments in 1 Timothy and followed the same pattern in Romans, where the ban on homosexual acts is based on the doctrine of creation. Those who appeal to love to justify homosexual acts argue that since homosexuals contribute to the realization of love among humans they should be encouraged, but the faulty nature of this position is seen in its foundational premise, for God's purpose for human fulfilment is not only that we love each other but also that we love God, and God cannot in one breath forbid homosexual behaviour and in the next permit it because it promotes human love.
keyPoints: Homosexuality has two meanings: attraction to members of one’s own sex, and same-sex genital acts
It comprises men and women; lesbianism is the female form; orientation differs from behaviour
The prohibitions make sense only in the light of the positive teaching of Genesis 1 and 2
Genesis 2 affirms the complementarity of the sexes as the basis of heterosexual marriage
Genesis 2:24 — the two become one flesh; the image is meaningless applied to homosexual relationships
Homosexual expression endangers sexual identity, the family and the stability of society
Jesus endorsed the Old Testament definition of marriage (Matt. 19:4-6, citing Gen. 1:27)
Heterosexual gender a divine creation, marriage a divine institution, fidelity a divine intention
The appeal to love fails, since God’s purpose is that we love him as well as one another

subject: CS
question: (a) Explain the term Society. (b) What are the essential characteristics of a society?
idealAnswer: Human beings are social animals: we live in communities that may be part of larger social groups called societies, and a personal being is never an isolated being, for our primary experience is that of living in relation with one another, sharing a whole set of values, perceptions, ideas and emotions; being born into and living with our family, race and nation is a fact of our human existence. A Society, therefore, is a group of people who conceive of themselves as distinct from other groups and who are connected together through communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics; what makes human societies different from groups of other social animals is that the members of human societies share a sense of common identity that grows out of their shared culture. Society may also be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good, and it is not a physical thing, for the only thing physical about Society is the members and their action. The essential characteristics are these. First, there can be no existing Society without members, and only rational and free beings can form a Society, since it is a union based on agreement about goals. Secondly, the members must be united in a stable or enduring way. Thirdly, the members must cooperate or work together for the attainment of some end, and this end will be some common good that all the members will share and that no member could accomplish singly. Fourthly, Society is held together by bonds, moral bonds of means and ends: either the members bind themselves by contract, pledge or agreement, or the bonds are imposed upon them by some law, natural or positive; it is this moral bond that distinguishes a Society from a crowd, which makes the individuals committed members and obliges them to their commitment. Finally, to guide the cooperative effort to the common good, Society must be equipped with that moral power called authority, which is the right to determine the means and direct the members in their use.

Only the members and their action are physical about a Society

Moral bonds distinguish a Society from a crowd

subject: CS
question: What is the role of the Church in sustaining democracy? Discuss any three (3).
idealAnswer: Democracy is by far the most politically friendly of all political ideologies of the state as far as the Church is concerned, and it is far better than its alternatives, especially communism and other dictatorships, since it ensures the type of constitution and government most conducive to the freedom and mission of the Church. Like the Church, however, democracy is not perfect, and just as the Church needs democracy for the smooth operation of her mission, democracy also needs the Church to overcome some of its weaknesses or to minimize their impact on society. Against the tyranny of democracy — the tendency of politicians to look out for the interest of the majority while neglecting the interest or abusing the rights of the minority, which is especially dangerous where the majority is of a particular racial, ethnic, religious or ideological orientation — the Church can help ensure that the government is fair to all its constituents and that minority rights and interests are protected as much as possible. Against the fallacy of democracy — the conceptual blunder of defending the tyranny of the majority by arguing that democracy is by definition the rule of the majority, when majority rule does not and should not imply minority suffering — the Church can help expose the error and ensure that the government is non-discriminatory but fair to all citizens irrespective of political affiliation, race, ethnicity, age or sex, which is supported by Paul's statement in Galatians 3:28 that there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles, between men and women, for all are one in union with Christ Jesus. Against the disease of democracy — the frequent election of representatives who make wonderful promises to their constituents, fail them, and attempt to help only when re-election approaches — the Church should educate her members and others on this selfish tendency and on studying political candidates very well before voting, and should train and encourage non-selfish, altruistic and mature Christians who are otherwise qualified to stand as candidates. Against red tapeism the Church can advise members in administration to minimize delays and to work as if working for God, and can organize experienced church leaders, superannuated clergy, lawyers and retired judges into "Christian Family Arbitration Centres" to settle cases out of court. Where democracy becomes a catalyst for ethnic conflicts, churches in conflict-prone areas must be part of the early warning system, informing security agents and preaching against ethnic conflict. Against the problem of vagueness in terms such as freedom, justice, equality and peace, the Church can sensitize people to the ambiguities and to their manipulation by political adventurers. Against vulnerability to military coups, whose common cause is corruption, the Church, through her military chaplains, guest preachers to the barracks and the mass media, should help all to see that corruption is part of human nature and cannot be removed by coups. In addition the Church prays for the state and supplements the government's efforts by establishing schools, vocational and technical institutes and agricultural research centres.

subject: CS
question: State and explain the five (5) principles of conflict resolution proposed by Tokunboh Adeyemo.
idealAnswer: In his article in the Africa Bible Commentary, Tokunboh Adeyemo writes that when we manage a conflict we simply organize, regulate and take charge of it in order to make it serve a good cause, and that in resolving any conflict there are three key questions to ask: what are we agreeing or disagreeing about; why are we agreeing or disagreeing; and how can we get past this and move forward? He proposes five principles which must guide us in resolving conflicts. The first is honest communication: silence and isolation deepen misunderstanding, which fuels conflict, and in Genesis 13:1-18 Abraham did not gloss over the potential for quarrels between his herdsmen and those of Lot, but discussed it openly with Lot and developed an appropriate strategy to deal with it. The second is getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives: often the apparent cause of a conflict is not the real issue, for the conflict is rooted in people's underlying motives and beliefs which they may not have clearly identified, and in Genesis 26:19-31 the real problem between the people of Gerar and Isaac went beyond water. The third is negotiation: the best way to find peace is through a process of give and take in which neither party to the conflict insists on being the winner, and the story of 1 Kings 12 shows the disastrous consequence of Rehoboam's unwillingness to negotiate. The fourth is external intervention: the parties involved may be so caught up in the conflict that they have difficulty talking to one another and reaching any agreement, and in such a case the assistance of a neutral person, such as a marriage counsellor, or of an organization like the United Nations may be sought, as in Acts 15:1-2 Paul and Barnabas and their opponents took their case to the apostles in Jerusalem. The fifth is divine intervention: there is a spiritual dimension to conflicts, so that in resolving them we need to seek divine assistance or intervention, and it was the Council at Jerusalem that resolved the crisis which would have permanently divided the church into Jews and Gentiles (Acts 15:23-29).

question: Write short notes on the following: i. Materialism. ii. Humanism. iii. Secularism.
idealAnswer: The three "isms" deal with the same thing, and in his book The Liberating Message — A Christian Worldview for Africa (1994) B. J. Van der Walt described secularism as the "mother of ideologies". Materialism is defined in the dictionary as the belief that only physical matter exists and the spiritual world does not, and such a believer is referred to as a materialist; according to Yusufu Turaki, materialism is another form of secularism, whereby people's lives are dominated by their desire for worldly pleasures and bodily comforts and revolve around money, possessions and the things of this world. Humanism is defined as a belief system based on the principle that people's spiritual and emotional needs can be fulfilled without following a god or religion, and such a believer is described as a humanist; secular humanism is likewise defined as a set of beliefs which emphasise the importance of reason and of individuals rather than religion. Secularism, as Yusufu Turaki writes in the Africa Bible Commentary, threatens the deeply religious African approach to all of life, being a Western philosophy which promotes a way of life and thought that is concerned only with this world and is opposed to thinking in terms of what is sacred or spiritual; it originated in Europe, in part as a reaction against the control of all areas of life by a church that was riddled with economic and political activities. Van der Walt adds that secularism did not intrude into Christianity from outside, since its germinating seed could already be discerned in the dualist Christianity of the Middle Ages when the church began to distinguish between the natural and the supernatural; instead of the Christian conquering the world, the world has conquered the Christian, and the process, though gradual — three centuries from the Renaissance and Humanism of the sixteenth century — has grown irresistibly, helped by the powers modern man has acquired: science, the power of knowledge; technology, the power of tools; and organization, the power of planning, integrating, co-ordinating and controlling. He concludes that secularism is the most dangerous enemy of Christianity, since it is not an open enemy attacking with physical weaponry but works practically unnoticed, infiltrating and undermining faith; it works gradually from the outside to the inside; and it is not a clearly discernible phenomenon but a chameleon ideology, the medium for the growth of a variety of other ideologies. The Bible's clear response to this way of life is found in Ecclesiastes, where Solomon on reflection found life to be "a chasing after the wind", and Turaki advises that religion provides ethical and social values that affect people in their private and public lives and makes for responsible living, so that Christians must exhibit their Christian life (Matt. 5:13-16) in secularized and materialistic societies in order to have influence.

topic: The Biblical Basis of Human Rights
question: According to John Stott the biblical bases of human rights hinges on three words. Briefly discuss each.
idealAnswer: John Stott begins by stating that the origin of human rights is creation: man has never acquired them, no government or other authority has conferred them, we have had them from the beginning, we received them with our life from our Maker, and they are inherent in our creation, having been bestowed on us by our Creator; fundamental to human rights, therefore, is the question of what it means to be human. On that foundation he hinges the Biblical basis of human rights on three words — dignity, equality and responsibility. Human dignity is based on Genesis 1:27-28, which deals with God's purpose for our creation, and three issues stand out. Our relationship to God: "God created man in his own image", so human beings have dignity because we are God-like beings created by God's will in his image, the divine image including those rational, moral and spiritual qualities which separate us from the animals and relate us to God. Our relationship to one another: "male and female he created them" — the God who made humankind is himself a social being, and it is clear that sexuality is God's creation, marriage is his institution and human companionship is his purpose, so that anyone who abuses these abuses God. Our relationship to the earth and its creatures: "fill the earth and subdue it" — God has given us dominion with instructions to subdue and cultivate the fruitful earth and rule its creatures, so that the rights to work and to rest, to share in the earth's resources, to food, clothing and shelter, to life and health, together with freedom from poverty, hunger and disease, all find their basis here. In addition to the dignity derived from our createdness, Christians can speak of the surpassing dignity derived from our Creator redeeming and recreating us through the incarnation and atonement of his Son. Human equality is the second word: the tragedy, Stott says, is that human rights have not always meant equal rights, for the good gifts of the Creator are spoiled by human selfishness, and the rights God gave to all human beings equally easily degenerate into my rights on which I insist, irrespective of the rights of others or of the common good. The God we worship shows no partiality, so in our attitude to other people we must show no partiality or give special deference to some because they are rich, famous or influential; Moses told Israel that the Lord shows no partiality and accepts no bribes, and Israelite judges were to do justice to the small and to the great alike (Deut. 10:17-18). All human rights violations contradict the equality we enjoy by creation, for "He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker" (Prov. 14:31). Human responsibility is the last word derived from our createdness: whenever human rights are emphasized to the exclusion of human responsibility we miss the Biblical pattern, and what we often hear is one person asserting his rights against another, which leads to conflict and encourages selfishness. The Bible calls us to defend other people's rights, but when it addresses us it emphasizes our responsibilities, not our rights: our responsibility is to secure the other person's rights, forgoing our own in order to do so. Jesus Christ is the supreme model of this renunciation of rights (Phil. 2:6-7), and Paul, who had rights as an apostle — the right to marry, the right to receive financial support — renounced them for the sake of the Gospel, to become everybody's slave and serve their rights (1 Cor. 9).

chapter: SEXUAL PERVERSION - WHAT IS THE BIBLICAL VIEW?
question: With scriptural supports explain why homosexuality is not biblical.
idealAnswer: The Bible says nothing about the homosexual orientation, but it condemns homosexual behaviour forthrightly. Sodom suffered God's judgement for threatened homosexual rape (Gen. 19:1-25; cf. Judges 19:11 — 20:48). In the Old Testament the Holiness Code of Leviticus labelled male homosexuals "detestable" and prescribed the death penalty for convicted offenders: "Do not lie with a man as one lies with a woman; that is detestable" (Lev. 18:22), and "If a man lies with a man as one lies with a woman, both of them have done what is detestable. They must be put to death" (Lev. 20:13). These prohibitions are not mere religious taboos, for they are connected with the prohibition of Deuteronomy 23:17 that no Israelite man or woman is to become a temple prostitute, the Canaanite fertility cult having included temple prostitution which promoted homosexuality; the death penalty prescribed shows the extreme seriousness with which homosexual practices were viewed. In the New Testament Paul condemns homosexual practice, including lesbianism, as unnatural, incompatible with the lifestyle of God's kingdom and an affront to God's law and gospel (Rom. 1:18-27; 1 Cor. 6:9-11; 1 Tim. 1:8-11). Romans 1:18-27 describes the idolatrous pagans of the Greco-Roman world who had a certain knowledge of God through the created universe and their own moral sense, yet ignored the truth in order to practise wickedness, turning to idols and confusing the Creator with the creatures, so that in judgement God gave them over to their depraved mind and decadent practices, including unnatural sex — men inflamed with lust for one another. Taken together, Paul's writings condemn homosexual behaviour as a vice of the Gentiles in Romans, as a bar to the Kingdom in Corinthians, and as an offence to be repudiated by the moral law in 1 Timothy. These prohibitions make sense only in the light of the positive teaching of Genesis 1 and 2 about human sexuality and heterosexual marriage: Genesis 2 affirms the complementarity of the sexes, for the human need for companionship is expressed in "It is not good for a man to be alone" (Gen. 2:18) and God met it by creating the woman out of the man, and the concluding comment is Genesis 2:24, "For this reason a man will leave his father and mother, and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh." The image of woman taken from man's flesh and becoming one flesh again with him is meaningless when applied to homosexual relationships, and homosexual expression endangers the formation of sexual identity in boys and girls, the integrity of the family and the stability of the whole society. In Matthew 19:4-6 Jesus himself endorsed the Old Testament definition of marriage with words from Genesis 1:27, affirming three truths: that heterosexual gender is a divine creation, that heterosexual marriage is a divine institution, and that heterosexual fidelity is a divine intention — so that a homosexual affair is a breach of all three. Nature and creation point the same way: to ask whether homosexuality is natural is to ask whether God made it, and the answer is no; Karl Barth points to how male and female complement each other as people created in the image of God, and Thomas Aquinas stresses that homosexual intercourse is by definition non-procreative and therefore cannot lead to full, secure family life. The early Church and the Reformers agreed: Tertullian, John Chrysostom and St. Augustine denounced such practices as unnatural, and Luther considered their toleration among the clergy one of the worst symptoms of decay in the church. Yet the syllabus insists that we must not come to this study with an attitude of moral superiority, since in God's view we are all sexual sinners, and homosexuals also are human beings who need to be loved back to Christ.

subject: CS
question: (a) What is the meaning of conflict? (b) Write short notes on Tokunboh Adeyemo’s five principles on resolving conflicts.
idealAnswer: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship, whether at home, at work, in the church or in the nation: when people come together regularly, especially where issues of personal significance are involved, differences emerge, and when conflict occurs between people, individually or in groups, they often become angry, hurt, bitter or defensive, so that the conflict sometimes ends the relationship or seriously damages it. While conflict is inevitable in relationships it can have either constructive or destructive results; conflicts sometimes measure the health of an organization, since in groups where nothing happens important enough to make people fight there is a greater chance of dying than in groups where dissension occurs; conflicts spotlight problems that require attention; and conflicts may force clarification of issues and challenge leaders to question the status quo and search for better solutions, as the good handling of the conflict between the Greeks and the Jews in the Early Church in Jerusalem resulted in the rapid growth of the Church (Acts 6:1-7). Conflict is also experienced within ourselves, as an inward personal struggle or restlessness of the soul. In his article in the Africa Bible Commentary, Tokunboh Adeyemo writes that when we manage a conflict we simply organize, regulate and take charge of it in order to make it serve a good cause, and he proposes five principles which must guide us in resolving conflicts. Honest communication: silence and isolation deepen misunderstanding, which fuels conflict, and Abraham did not gloss over the potential for quarrels between his herdsmen and Lot's but discussed it openly and developed an appropriate strategy (Gen. 13:1-18). Getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives: often the apparent cause of a conflict is not the real issue, which is rooted in people's underlying motives and beliefs, as the real problem between the people of Gerar and Isaac went beyond water (Gen. 26:19-31). Negotiation: the best way to find peace is through a process of give and take in which neither party insists on being the winner, and 1 Kings 12 shows the disastrous consequence of Rehoboam's unwillingness to negotiate. External intervention: where the parties are so caught up in the conflict that they cannot talk to one another, the assistance of a neutral person such as a marriage counsellor, or of an organization like the United Nations, may be sought, as Paul and Barnabas and their opponents took their case to the apostles in Jerusalem (Acts 15:1-2). Divine intervention: there is a spiritual dimension to conflicts, so in resolving them we need to seek divine assistance, and the Council at Jerusalem resolved the crisis that would have permanently divided the church into Jews and Gentiles (Acts 15:23-29).
keyPoints: Conflict is a fact of life in any ongoing relationship
It may have constructive or destructive results and may measure the health of an organization
Adeyemo: to manage a conflict is to organize, regulate and take charge of it to serve a good cause
Honest communication — Abraham and Lot (Gen. 13:1-18)
Getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives — Isaac and Gerar (Gen. 26:19-31)
Negotiation — Rehoboam (1 Kings 12)
External intervention — Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:1-2)

subject: CS
question: State and explain any four (4) essential characteristics of a society.
idealAnswer: Society may be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good; it is not a physical thing, for the only thing physical about Society is the members and their action. From that definition its essential characteristics follow. First, membership: there can be no existing Society without members, and only rational and free beings can form a Society, since it is a union based on agreement about goals — which is why a herd of animals is not a society. Secondly, stability: the members must be united in a stable or enduring way, so that a chance gathering of people is not a society. Thirdly, cooperation for a common end: the members must cooperate or work together for the attainment of some end, and this end will be some common good that all the members will share and that no member could accomplish singly. Fourthly, moral bonds: Society is held together by bonds, moral bonds of means and ends — either the members bind themselves by contract, pledge or agreement, or the bonds are imposed upon them by some law, natural or positive — and it is this moral bond that distinguishes a Society from a crowd, which makes the individuals committed members and obliges them to their commitment. Fifthly, authority: to guide the cooperative effort to the common good, Society must be equipped with that moral power called authority, authority being the right to determine the means and direct the members in their use.

The end is a common good no member could accomplish singly

The moral bond distinguishes a Society from a crowd

subject: CS
question: (a) What is a society? (b) Advance 4 reasons to defend why humans must live in societies.
idealAnswer: A Society is a group of people who conceive of themselves as distinct from other groups and who are connected together through communication ties, common customs and traditions, and institutions such as politics, law and economics; what makes human societies different from groups of other social animals is that their members share a sense of common identity that grows out of their shared culture. Society may also be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good. Human beings are social animals, and we live in communities that may be part of these larger social groups; a personal being is never an isolated being, for our primary experience is that of living in relation with one another, sharing a whole set of values, perceptions, ideas and emotions, and being born into and living with our family, race and nation is a fact of our human existence. Four reasons may be given why humans must live in societies. First, people abhor solitude and crave companionship: we spontaneously seek others and enjoy their company, whereas loneliness sets up a veritable hunger in the soul. Secondly, we cannot take care of ourselves alone: the child must be reared by the parents for many years, without the family no children grow up, and living in the family implies cooperation right from the beginning of each one's life. Thirdly, the gift of language fits us to communicate with one another, to discuss projects of common interest and to agree on means and ends for cooperative effort, so that the ability of speech itself indicates that we are meant to live a social life. Fourthly, intellectual and moral development requires the constant communication of ideas and values among people, an exchange possible only in a Society. Society is therefore essential to humans, and Aristotle is right in saying that "the life of solitude is fit only for a beast or a god".

Members share a sense of common identity from a shared culture

We cannot take care of ourselves alone; the child must be reared by parents
The gift of language fits us to communicate and cooperate
Intellectual and moral development requires an exchange possible only in a Society

subject: CS
topic: The Position of the Methodist Church Ghana
question: State the Methodist Church Ghana’s position on divorce and remarriage as found in S. O. 743.
idealAnswer: The Church's position is found in Standing Order 743 of the Constitution, under the title Divorce, Dissolution of Marriage and Remarriage. First, no member of the Church shall dissolve his or her marriage without first consulting his or her Minister, who shall make every effort to reconcile the parties and shall, if need be, seek the assistance of the Leaders' Meeting. Secondly, if one partner fails in fulfilling the obligations of marriage, it is the duty of the other, as a Christian, to be active in seeking reconciliation so long as any possibility of it remains. Thirdly, where all efforts to effect reconciliation fail, the Leaders' Meeting shall be informed of this. Fourthly, when one party has already formed a union with a third person and is judged to be beyond hope of restoration to the lawful partner, the latter may be permitted to dissolve the marriage by the appropriate process under the Ordinance or Customary Law, and shall then be free to re-marry in due course; this permission to divorce and re-marry shall be subject to confirmation by the Bishop of the Diocese, who shall act in consultation with the Circuit Superintendent concerned and a small committee, including a lawyer, appointed by Synod. Finally, any member who dissolves his or her marriage against the advice of the Minister and the Leaders' Meeting, or who is the guilty party in divorce proceedings, or who contravenes S.O. 742 (3) (1), shall be subject to the discipline of the Leaders' Meeting. These provisions are quoted from the Constitution and Standing Orders of the Methodist Church Ghana, 2000 Revised Edition. Behind them lies the "peace" or "freedom" principle: the principle that "God has called us to live in peace or freedom", established by Paul in 1 Corinthians 7:15 as a basis for divorce in mixed-faith marriages, may be extended to other cases after all efforts have been made to save a marriage, and this appears to be the spirit of S.O. 743.

subject: CS
chapter: RELIGIOUS PLURALISM AND THE CHRISTIAN MESSAGE
question: (a) Define Secularism. (b) State the three (3) reasons given by Van der Walt for describing Secularism as the most dangerous enemy of Christianity.
idealAnswer: Secularism, as Yusufu Turaki writes in the Africa Bible Commentary, is the Western philosophy which threatens the deeply religious African approach to all of life, promoting a way of life and thought that is concerned only with this world and is opposed to thinking in terms of what is sacred or spiritual; it originated in Europe, in part as a reaction against the control of all areas of life by a church that was riddled with the economic and political activities of a country. B. J. Van der Walt, in The Liberating Message — A Christian Worldview for Africa (1994), calls secularism the "mother of ideologies", noting that it did not intrude into Christianity from outside, since its germinating seed could already be discerned in the dualist Christianity of the Middle Ages when the church began to distinguish between the natural and the supernatural, between aspects of life that involved God and those that did not; instead of the Christian conquering the world, the world has conquered the Christian. Van der Walt concludes his discussion by describing secularism as the most dangerous enemy of Christianity, drawing attention to the conclusion of the World Mission Conference held in Jerusalem in 1982, that the greatest rival of Christianity in the world today is not Mohammedanism, Buddhism, Hinduism or Confucianism, but a worldwide secular way of life and interpretation of the nature of things. He gives three reasons in support of that statement. First, secularism is not an open enemy attacking the Christian faith with physical weaponry; it works practically unnoticed, and in a subtle way it infiltrates and undermines faith. Secondly, it works gradually from the outside to the inside: from the outside it might seem as if the Christian faith is still in order while living communion with God has in reality ceased to exist, and the process is so gradual that mostly we do not notice it any more, so that when we ultimately realize that an institution or the whole of life has been secularized it is already too late. Thirdly, it is not a clearly discernible and definable phenomenon: it is a sort of chameleon ideology, the medium for the growth of a variety of ideologies which in turn further promote the process of secularization. Van der Walt believes we should neither under-estimate nor over-estimate the power of secularism, because the Gospel of Jesus Christ has power to conquer it, and he is convinced that only a radical, total, integral Christian worldview will be able to break the formidable power of secularism — not only in theory but concretely, in family life, in education, in politics, in the world of commerce and labour and even in the church.

subject: CS
topic: INTRODUCTION: THE NATURE OF HUMAN RIGHTS
question: State and explain the four (4) basic human needs according to Galting.
idealAnswer: We are used to thinking about human rights in terms of freedom from specific abuses or restrictions, especially by governments, but there is a more comprehensive concept of rights, holding that peoples and groups not only have the right not to be specifically abused but also have rights to a quality of life that at a minimum does not detract from their human dignity. One scholar suggests that the most fruitful way to think about human rights is to begin with the idea that ultimately they are supposed to serve basic human needs (Galting, 1994), and according to Galting the basic human needs which generate corresponding rights are four. Survival needs, to avoid violence: this is the right to be free from individual and collective violence. Well-being needs, to avoid misery: the right to adequate nutrition and water; to movement, sleep, sex and other biological wants; to protection from diseases and from adverse climatological and environmental impacts. Identity needs, to avoid alienation: the right to self-expression; to realize one's potential; to establish and maintain emotional bonds with others; to preserve cultural heritage and association; to contribute through work and other activity; and to receive information about and maintain contact with nature, the global humanity and other aspects of the biosphere. Freedom needs, to avoid repression: the right to receive and express opinions, to assemble with others, to have a common policy, and to choose from a wide range in such matters as jobs, spouse, where to live and life style.

Survival needs — to avoid violence: freedom from individual and collective violence
Well-being needs — to avoid misery: nutrition, water, movement, sleep, protection from disease
Identity needs — to avoid alienation: self-expression, potential, emotional bonds, cultural heritage
Freedom needs — to avoid repression: opinion, assembly, common policy, choice of job, spouse and lifestyle
